title: Motion in a Plane
description: Class 11 Physics Motion in a Plane: vectors and their operations, projectile motion, range and uniform circular motion with diagrams, solved numericals and tests.

topics.title: Vectors & Their Operations
topics.concept:
In Class 9 you described motion along a straight line, where direction could be handled with a simple plus or minus sign. Motion in a plane is richer: a cricket ball arcs across the field, a swimmer drifts across a river. To handle two dimensions we need a tool that carries both magnitude and direction together — and that tool is the vector.

Physical quantities fall into two families. A scalar has only magnitude: mass, time, temperature, speed, distance and energy are all scalars and obey ordinary arithmetic. A vector has both magnitude and direction and follows special rules of addition: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum are vectors. A vector is drawn as an arrow whose length is its magnitude and whose head points in its direction. We write it as $\vec{A}$ and its magnitude as $|\vec{A}|$ or simply $A$.

Two vectors are added head to tail. In the triangle law, the tail of $\vec{B}$ is placed at the head of $\vec{A}$, and the arrow drawn from the tail of $\vec{A}$ to the head of $\vec{B}$ is the resultant $\vec{R}=\vec{A}+\vec{B}$. The parallelogram law states that if two vectors acting at a point are the adjacent sides of a parallelogram, the diagonal through that point is their resultant. When $\vec{A}$ and $\vec{B}$ have an angle $\theta$ between them, the magnitude of the resultant is $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}$, and it makes an angle $\alpha$ with $\vec{A}$ where $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}$.

Working with arrows geometrically is clumsy, so we resolve each vector into perpendicular components along the x and y axes. Using the unit vectors $\hat{i}$ (along x) and $\hat{j}$ (along y), a vector making angle $\theta$ with the x-axis becomes $\vec{A}=A\cos\theta\,\hat{i}+A\sin\theta\,\hat{j}$. A unit vector has magnitude exactly 1 and only fixes direction; $\hat{A}=\dfrac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}$. To add vectors by components, simply add the x-parts and the y-parts separately. Two ways of multiplying vectors also appear: the dot (scalar) product $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=AB\cos\theta$ gives a scalar (used for work), while the cross (vector) product $\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=AB\sin\theta\,\hat{n}$ gives a vector perpendicular to both (used for torque).

  • Scalar: magnitude only (mass, speed, time, distance).
  • Vector: magnitude and direction (displacement, velocity, force).
  • Resultant: $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}$ with $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{B\sin\theta}{A+B\cos\theta}$.
  • Components: $A_x=A\cos\theta$, $A_y=A\sin\theta$; magnitude $A=\sqrt{A_x^2+A_y^2}$.
  • Products: dot $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=AB\cos\theta$ (scalar); cross $|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=AB\sin\theta$ (vector).

examples.problem: Two forces of $3\,\text{N}$ and $4\,\text{N}$ act at right angles ($\theta=90^\circ$) to each other at a point. Find the magnitude of their resultant.
A vector $\vec{A}$ of magnitude $10\,\text{units}$ makes an angle of $30^\circ$ with the x-axis. Find its x and y components.
Two forces of equal magnitude $F$ act at an angle of $60^\circ$. The resultant has magnitude $\sqrt{3}\,F$. Verify this using the parallelogram law.
Find the magnitude of the vector $\vec{A}=6\,\hat{i}+8\,\hat{j}$ and the unit vector along it.
Two vectors of magnitudes $5\,\text{units}$ and $5\,\text{units}$ act with an angle of $90^\circ$ between them. Find the magnitude of their cross product.

recap: A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has both magnitude and direction.
Vectors add head to tail using the triangle or parallelogram law: $R=\sqrt{A^2+B^2+2AB\cos\theta}$.
Any vector resolves into components $A_x=A\cos\theta$, $A_y=A\sin\theta$, written with unit vectors $\hat{i},\hat{j}$.
A unit vector $\hat{A}=\dfrac{\vec{A}}{|\vec{A}|}$ has magnitude 1 and fixes only direction.
Dot product $\vec{A}\cdot\vec{B}=AB\cos\theta$ gives a scalar; cross product $|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=AB\sin\theta$ gives a vector.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a vector quantity?
quiz.explanation: Force has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Speed, mass and temperature are scalars.

quiz.q: Two forces of 6 N and 8 N act at right angles. Their resultant is:
quiz.explanation: At 90 degrees, R = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = sqrt(100) = 10 N.

quiz.q: The x-component of a vector A making angle theta with the x-axis is:
quiz.explanation: The component along the x-axis is the adjacent side, A cos theta.

quiz.q: The magnitude of a unit vector is always:
quiz.explanation: A unit vector has magnitude exactly 1 and only specifies direction.

topics.title: Projectile Motion
topics.concept:
Throw a stone at an angle and watch it: it rises, curves over and falls in a graceful arch. Any object thrown into the air that then moves only under gravity (we ignore air resistance) is called a projectile, and its curved path is its trajectory. The whole subject of projectile motion rests on one brilliant idea — the horizontal and vertical motions are completely independent of each other and can be analysed separately.

Suppose the projectile is launched with speed $u$ at an angle $\theta$ above the horizontal. We split this into a horizontal part $u_x=u\cos\theta$ and a vertical part $u_y=u\sin\theta$. Horizontally there is no acceleration, so the horizontal velocity stays constant: $x=u\cos\theta\cdot t$. Vertically the only force is gravity, giving a constant downward acceleration $g$, so $y=u\sin\theta\cdot t-\tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. Eliminating $t$ between these gives the equation of the path: $y=x\tan\theta-\dfrac{g\,x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$, which is the equation of a parabola. So every projectile traces a parabola.

Three quantities describe the flight. The time of flight $T$ is how long the projectile stays in the air; since the vertical velocity must reverse and the projectile returns to launch height, $T=\dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$. The maximum height $H$ is reached when the vertical velocity becomes zero: $H=\dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$. The horizontal range $R$ is the horizontal distance covered in the total time of flight: $R=u\cos\theta\cdot T=\dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$.

A neat consequence: range is maximum when $\sin 2\theta=1$, i.e. $\theta=45^\circ$, giving $R_{max}=\dfrac{u^2}{g}$. Also, two angles that add up to $90^\circ$ (like $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$) give the same range. A special case is the horizontal projectile — an object thrown horizontally with speed $u$ from a height $h$. Here $u_y=0$ initially, so the time to fall is $t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$ and the horizontal range is $R=u\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$, while its path is still half a parabola.

  • Path: a parabola, $y=x\tan\theta-\dfrac{g\,x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$.
  • Time of flight: $T=\dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$.
  • Maximum height: $H=\dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$.
  • Range: $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$; maximum at $\theta=45^\circ$ where $R_{max}=\dfrac{u^2}{g}$.
  • Horizontal projectile from height $h$: $t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$, $R=u\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

examples.problem: A ball is projected at $20\,\text{m/s}$ at an angle of $30^\circ$ to the horizontal. Find its time of flight. (Take $g=10\,\text{m/s}^2$.)
For the same ball ($u=20\,\text{m/s}$, $\theta=30^\circ$, $g=10\,\text{m/s}^2$), find the maximum height reached.
A projectile is fired at $u=40\,\text{m/s}$ at $45^\circ$. Find its horizontal range. (Take $g=10\,\text{m/s}^2$.)
examples.solution:
1. $R=\dfrac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$ with $2\theta=90^\circ$, so $\sin 90^\circ=1$.
  2. $R=\dfrac{40^2\times 1}{10}=\dfrac{1600}{10}$.
  3. $=160\,\text{m}$ (this is also the maximum possible range for this speed).

Answer: Range $=160\,\text{m}$.

examples.problem: A stone is thrown at $u=10\,\text{m/s}$ at $60^\circ$. Find its range. (Take $g=10\,\text{m/s}^2$, $\sin 120^\circ=\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.)
An object is thrown horizontally at $u=15\,\text{m/s}$ from a cliff $20\,\text{m}$ high. Find the time to reach the ground. (Take $g=10\,\text{m/s}^2$.)
examples.solution:
1. Vertical motion only: $t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$ with $h=20\,\text{m}$.
  2. $t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2\times 20}{10}}=\sqrt{4}$.
  3. $=2\,\text{s}$ (independent of the horizontal speed).

Answer: Time to land $=2\,\text{s}$.

examples.problem: For the horizontal projectile above ($u=15\,\text{m/s}$, $h=20\,\text{m}$, $t=2\,\text{s}$), find the horizontal distance covered before landing.
examples.solution:
1. Horizontal velocity is constant, so $R=u\cdot t$.
  2. $R=15\times 2$.
  3. $=30\,\text{m}$.

Answer: Horizontal distance $=30\,\text{m}$.

recap: A projectile moves under gravity alone; its horizontal and vertical motions are independent.
For a horizontal projectile from height $h$: $t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$ and $R=u\sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$.

quiz.q: The path (trajectory) of a projectile is a:
quiz.explanation: Eliminating time between horizontal and vertical equations gives y as a quadratic in x, i.e. a parabola.

quiz.q: The horizontal range of a projectile is maximum when the angle of projection is:
quiz.explanation: R = u^2 sin(2 theta)/g is maximum when sin(2 theta) = 1, i.e. 2 theta = 90, so theta = 45 degrees.

quiz.q: During projectile motion, the horizontal component of velocity:
quiz.explanation: There is no horizontal acceleration, so u cos theta stays constant throughout the flight.

quiz.q: At the highest point of its path, a projectile's vertical velocity is:
quiz.explanation: At maximum height the upward motion stops momentarily, so the vertical velocity is zero (only the horizontal part remains).

topics.title: Uniform Circular Motion
topics.concept:
A stone tied to a string and whirled overhead, the tip of a fan blade, a satellite circling the Earth — all move along a circular path. When an object moves in a circle at constant speed, we call it uniform circular motion. The word uniform refers to the speed, not the velocity: even though the speed never changes, the direction of motion changes at every instant, so the velocity changes — which means the object is always accelerating.

Instead of measuring distance along the arc, it is easier to measure the angle swept at the centre. This is the angular displacement $\theta$, measured in radians (one full circle is $2\pi$ radians). The rate at which this angle is swept is the angular velocity $\omega=\dfrac{\theta}{t}$, with SI unit radian per second ($\text{rad/s}$). The ordinary (linear) speed $v$ along the circle of radius $r$ is linked to angular velocity by the simple and important relation $v=\omega r$.

Circular motion repeats itself, so we describe it with two more quantities. The time period $T$ is the time for one complete revolution, and the frequency $f$ is the number of revolutions per second, with $f=\dfrac{1}{T}$ (unit hertz, $\text{Hz}$). In one period the object sweeps $2\pi$ radians, so $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi f$. These let us convert easily between revolutions, angles and time.

The most important idea is the acceleration. Because the velocity continuously changes direction, there is an acceleration directed at every instant towards the centre of the circle. This is the centripetal acceleration $a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}=\omega^2 r$. The word centripetal means centre-seeking. The force that produces it — tension in the string, gravity for a satellite, friction for a car turning — is the centripetal force $F_c=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=m\omega^2 r$, always directed towards the centre. Without it, the object would fly off along a tangent in a straight line, exactly as Newton's first law predicts.

  • Uniform circular motion: constant speed, continuously changing direction (so the velocity changes).
  • Angular velocity: $\omega=\dfrac{\theta}{t}$, unit rad/s; linked to speed by $v=\omega r$.
  • Period and frequency: $f=\dfrac{1}{T}$ and $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=2\pi f$.
  • Centripetal acceleration: $a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}=\omega^2 r$, directed towards the centre.
  • Centripetal force: $F_c=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=m\omega^2 r$, also towards the centre.

examples.problem: A particle moves in a circle of radius $0.5\,\text{m}$ with a constant speed of $4\,\text{m/s}$. Find its centripetal acceleration.
A body completes one revolution of a circle in $4\,\text{s}$. Find its angular velocity. (Take $\pi=3.14$.)
An object moves in a circle of radius $2\,\text{m}$ with angular velocity $3\,\text{rad/s}$. Find its linear speed.
A wheel rotates at $120\,\text{revolutions per minute (rpm)}$. Find its frequency in $\text{Hz}$ and its time period.
A stone of mass $0.2\,\text{kg}$ is whirled in a circle of radius $1\,\text{m}$ at $5\,\text{m/s}$. Find the centripetal force.
A particle in a circle of radius $0.25\,\text{m}$ has angular velocity $4\,\text{rad/s}$. Find its centripetal acceleration using $a_c=\omega^2 r$.

recap: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the direction (and hence velocity) changes continuously.
Angular velocity $\omega=\dfrac{\theta}{t}$ (rad/s) links to linear speed by $v=\omega r$.
Centripetal acceleration $a_c=\dfrac{v^2}{r}=\omega^2 r$ always points towards the centre.
The centripetal force $F_c=\dfrac{mv^2}{r}=m\omega^2 r$ keeps the body on its circular path.

quiz.q: In uniform circular motion, which quantity stays constant?
quiz.explanation: The speed is constant, but the direction (and so the velocity and the direction of acceleration) keeps changing.

quiz.q: The centripetal acceleration of a body in a circle of radius r at speed v is:
quiz.explanation: Centripetal acceleration a_c = v^2 / r = omega^2 r, directed towards the centre.

quiz.q: The relation between linear speed v and angular velocity omega is:
quiz.explanation: Linear speed equals angular velocity times the radius: v = omega r.

quiz.q: The centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion is always directed:
quiz.explanation: Centripetal means centre-seeking; the acceleration points towards the centre of the circle at all times.

online.title: Motion in a Plane — Online Test

questions.q: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
questions.explanation: Mass has only magnitude, so it is a scalar.

questions.q: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act at right angles. The resultant is:
The y-component of a vector A making angle theta with the x-axis is:
questions.explanation: The component along the y-axis is A sin theta.

questions.q: The magnitude of a unit vector is:
questions.explanation: A unit vector always has magnitude 1.

questions.q: The path of a projectile (ignoring air resistance) is a:
questions.explanation: Eliminating time gives y as a quadratic in x, so the path is a parabola.

questions.q: The horizontal range of a projectile is maximum at a projection angle of:
questions.explanation: R = u^2 sin(2 theta)/g is maximum when sin(2 theta) = 1, i.e. theta = 45 degrees.

questions.q: During projectile motion, the horizontal velocity component:
questions.explanation: There is no horizontal acceleration, so u cos theta is constant throughout.

questions.q: At the highest point of a projectile's path, its vertical velocity is:
questions.explanation: At maximum height the vertical motion momentarily stops, so the vertical velocity is zero.

questions.q: A ball is projected at 20 m/s at 30 degrees. Its time of flight (g = 10 m/s^2) is:
questions.explanation: T = 2u sin theta/g = 2 x 20 x 0.5 / 10 = 2 s.

questions.q: A projectile fired at 40 m/s at 45 degrees has a range (g = 10 m/s^2) of:
In uniform circular motion, the quantity that remains constant is:
questions.explanation: Only the speed is constant; the velocity changes because the direction changes.

questions.q: The centripetal acceleration of a body moving at speed v in a circle of radius r is:
questions.explanation: a_c = v^2 / r = omega^2 r, directed towards the centre.

questions.q: The relation between linear speed and angular velocity is:
questions.explanation: Linear speed v = omega r.

questions.q: The centripetal force on a body moving in a circle is directed:
questions.explanation: Centripetal force always points towards the centre of the circle.

questions.q: A particle moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m at 4 m/s. Its centripetal acceleration is:
The angular velocity of a body completing one revolution in 4 s (pi = 3.14) is:
questions.explanation: omega = 2 pi / T = 6.28 / 4 = 1.57 rad/s.

questions.q: The dot product of two perpendicular vectors is:
questions.explanation: A . B = AB cos 90 = 0, since cos 90 = 0.

questions.q: Two angles of projection that give the same range are:
questions.explanation: Angles adding to 90 degrees give the same range; 30 + 60 = 90.

questions.q: An object thrown horizontally from a 20 m tower (g = 10 m/s^2) reaches the ground in:
questions.explanation: t = sqrt(2h/g) = sqrt(40/10) = sqrt(4) = 2 s.

questions.q: A wheel rotating at 120 rpm has a frequency of:
questions.explanation: f = 120/60 = 2 revolutions per second = 2 Hz.

imo.title: Motion in a Plane — Olympiad Test

questions.q: Two equal forces give a resultant equal to one of them in magnitude. The angle between them is:
questions.explanation: R^2 = F^2 + F^2 + 2F^2 cos theta = F^2 gives cos theta = -1/2, so theta = 120 degrees.

questions.q: If A = i + j and B = i - j, the angle between A and B is:
questions.explanation: A . B = (1)(1) + (1)(-1) = 0, so the vectors are perpendicular (90 degrees).

questions.q: A projectile has the same range for angles of 15 degrees and another angle. That angle is:
questions.explanation: Complementary angles give equal range: 15 + 75 = 90 degrees.

questions.q: At the top of its path, a projectile launched at u and theta has speed:
questions.explanation: Vertical velocity is zero at the top; only the horizontal part u cos theta remains.

questions.q: The maximum height of a projectile equals its range when tan theta equals:
questions.explanation: H = R gives (u^2 sin^2 theta)/(2g) = (u^2 sin 2 theta)/g, leading to tan theta = 4.

questions.q: A body in uniform circular motion has its acceleration and velocity at an angle of:
questions.explanation: Velocity is tangential and centripetal acceleration points to the centre, so they are perpendicular (90 degrees).

questions.q: If the speed of a body in a circle doubles (radius unchanged), its centripetal acceleration becomes:
questions.explanation: a_c is proportional to v^2, so doubling v makes a_c four times larger.

questions.q: A particle moves with v = omega r. If omega is halved and r is doubled, the linear speed becomes:
questions.explanation: v = omega r; (omega/2)(2r) = omega r, so the speed is unchanged.

questions.q: Two projectiles are fired with the same speed at 30 and 60 degrees. The ratio of their maximum heights H(30) : H(60) is:
questions.explanation: H is proportional to sin^2 theta; sin^2 30 : sin^2 60 = (1/4) : (3/4) = 1 : 3.

questions.q: The magnitude of the change in velocity of a body moving with speed v through a quarter circle is:
questions.explanation: Initial and final velocities are perpendicular and equal in magnitude, so |delta v| = sqrt(v^2 + v^2) = v sqrt(2).

questions.q: An object thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from a 45 m cliff lands at a horizontal distance of (g = 10 m/s^2):
The resultant of two vectors is maximum when the angle between them is:
questions.explanation: R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta) is maximum when cos theta = 1, i.e. theta = 0 (R = A + B).

questions.q: A car turns on a circular track of radius 50 m at 10 m/s. The centripetal acceleration is:
For a projectile, the velocity is minimum:
questions.explanation: At the highest point the vertical component is zero, so the speed (only u cos theta) is minimum.
